questions.q: What does this lesson say about most job postings' requirement lists?
options: They usually describe a hiring manager's ideal candidate, not a strict minimum bar, so requirements should be sorted into must-have and nice-to-have instead of treated as one pass/fail gate
Every requirement listed is always mandatory and disqualifying
Job postings never list any requirements at all
Nice-to-have items always matter more than required items
questions.explain: Most postings list more than any real candidate will have. Sorting requirements into must-have and nice-to-have, based on their phrasing, is how you judge realistic fit.

questions.q: Which phrasing typically signals a nice-to-have requirement rather than a must-have one?
options: "Preferred," "a plus," "familiarity with"
"Required"
"Must have"
A specific years-of-experience threshold tied to the core skill
questions.explain: Language like "preferred," "a plus," or "familiarity with" signals a helpful-but-not-disqualifying requirement, unlike "required" or "must have" language.

questions.q: How can a candidate tell that a posting titled "BI Developer" is really asking for a different specialization, like data engineering?
options: By reading past the title into the body of responsibilities — heavy emphasis on Python, cloud pipeline tools, and data-engineering language with reporting only mentioned in passing is a sign
The job title alone always tells you exactly what the role needs
By checking whether the company's name sounds technical
By assuming every posting means exactly what its title says
questions.explain: The actual body of a posting — not just its title — reveals what the role is really asking for. Heavy data-engineering language with reporting as an afterthought signals a data engineering role wearing a BI title.

questions.q: Which of these is a red flag this lesson identifies in a job posting?
options: Expert-level requirements stacked across five or six unrelated tools at a junior-sounding salary
A clearly stated salary range
Responsibilities described in specific, concrete detail
A requirements list that distinguishes required from preferred skills
questions.explain: Unrealistic requirement stacking usually signals a role that was never properly scoped. A clear salary range and specific, well-differentiated requirements are the opposite of a red flag.

questions.q: What does "keyword mapping" mean in the context of reading job postings, according to this lesson?
options: Translating a posting's vocabulary (like "ETL" or "data pipelines") to your own resume language (like SSIS) to judge real fit
Copying every keyword from the posting directly into your resume without changes
Ignoring the posting's wording entirely
Only applying to postings that use the exact same tool names as your resume
questions.explain: A posting's exact vocabulary and a resume's exact vocabulary rarely match word for word — mapping the posting's phrasing to your actual skills (SSIS to "ETL," Power BI to "BI tools") is what lets you judge real fit correctly.
